title: Before optimizing, check the three things it depends on: the model, the objective and the gradient
summary: A penalized-flow model, a dissipated-power identity and an analytic gradient checked against finite differences are the standard pre-flight tests of a density-based topology optimization. Each figure is a check with a pass criterion; read how large the discrepancy is, against what, and how it changes with the penalty and the mesh.

media.alt: Two panels against the Brinkman friction parameter alpha on a log axis from 1 to 1e10, for two meshes. Left: mean speed inside the penalized disc falls steadily from about 1 metre per second to about 1e-7 to 1e-6 metres per second, and is lower on the finer mesh. Right: percent velocity mismatch against a body-fitted mesh drops from about 65 percent at alpha = 1 to a minimum of about 1 to 1.5 percent near alpha = 1e4 to 1e6 (stars) and rises again at larger alpha, with the fine mesh lower. A long footnote explains the minimum.

source.note: Standard density-based (Brinkman) topology optimization concepts only; the figures show no optimized designs or objective values, only the pre-optimization checks.

read_the_figure.question: Is each ingredient of the optimization (penalized flow model, dissipation objective, analytic gradient) correct on its own, before any design is optimized?
read_the_figure.axes: Exact profiles: x is position across a 20 micrometre channel, y is velocity in m/s, one curve per penalization strength alpha. Penalization vs body-fitted: x is alpha on a log axis in Pa s per square metre, y is leak speed inside the penalized region (log axis, left) or percent mismatch outside it (right), for two mesh sizes. Dissipation identity: two bars for each of two viscous-term forms, in W per metre of depth. Gradient check: x is the design strip index, y on the left is the sensitivity dPhi/d alpha_e, on the right the relative error on a log axis against a 1e-6 reference line.
look_at: Exact profiles: the black Poiseuille parabola flattens and falls in height as alpha grows, because the penalty acts like added friction.
Left panel of the comparison: the straight descent on log-log axes, lower on the finer mesh, means the penalized region becomes more solid-like at a rate set by alpha.
Right panel: the mismatch has a minimum (stars) and then rises, and the minimum moves to larger alpha and smaller value on the finer mesh.
Identity bars: the blue and grey bars should be equal; the printed percentages E give the difference.
Gradient check: the red crosses lie on the blue markers, and the errors on the right sit far below the 1e-6 line.
read_the_figure.proves: The exact profile validates the model equation that the optimization solves. The identity shows the objective is computed consistently by two routes. The gradient check shows the derivative that the optimizer uses is the derivative of the function it evaluates. Together they certify the ingredients, not the optimum.
if_wrong: A mismatch that grows with alpha, as here, on a fixed mesh: a conditioning or resolution floor of the penalization, not a modelling error; the footnote shows it moves with the mesh.
Bars that differ by more than discretization error: the objective is inconsistent with the physics, for example a missing term.
Gradient errors of order 1e-3 or more that do not improve with step size: a derivation or assembly error. Errors that grow when the step is made much smaller: round-off in the difference.
Leak speed that does not fall with alpha: the penalty is not applied in the region.
must_check: The tolerance of each pass criterion (the figures draw 1e-6 on two of them).
Mesh refinement is shown for any discrepancy attributed to resolution.
Both step sizes of the finite difference are shown, to rule out truncation and round-off together.
Which viscous form is used in the objective and the state equation.
The dimension of the quantities (power per unit depth for a 2D problem).
as_drawn: Exact profiles (alpha = 0, 3e6, 1e7, 5e7): peak velocity about 0.0050, 0.0044, 0.0035 and 0.0016 m/s on a channel from -10 to +10 micrometres. A pass label reports ODE residual below 1e-6 relative for all alpha.

Comparison: leak speed falls from about 1 m/s at alpha = 1 to about 5e-7 m/s (coarse mesh) and 2e-8 m/s (fine mesh) at alpha = 1e10. Outside mismatch is about 65 percent at alpha = 1, with minimum about 1.46 percent near 1e4 on the coarse mesh and about 1.04 percent near 1e6 on the fine mesh, per the footnote, rising to about 7 percent and 2.4 percent at alpha = 1e10.
Identity: bars of about 1.37e-7 W/m for each form; the errors printed are 0.08 percent and 0.18 percent.
Gradient: dPhi/d alpha_e about 1.38e-15 to 1.44e-15 m^4/s^2 across six strips; relative error about 1e-11 to 5e-11 for h_rel = 0.001 and about 1e-10 to 2e-10 for h_rel = 0.01.

terms.meaning: A friction term alpha u added to the momentum equation. Large alpha forces the velocity towards zero, so a region with large alpha behaves like a solid inside a fluid mesh.
Optimizing a field alpha(x) between fluid-like and solid-like values to minimize an objective subject to the flow equations, introduced for Stokes flow by Borrvall and Petersson.
A mesh whose cells follow the boundary of the solid, so no penalization is needed.
The mechanical power converted to heat by viscous and Brinkman friction, the standard objective for minimum-pressure-drop designs.
The derivative of the objective with respect to a design variable, here the penalty in element e.
Comparing an analytic derivative with (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h for small h.

remember: Always check the gradient of an optimization problem against finite differences before running the optimizer.
An error that falls with refinement is discretization; one that does not is modelling or coding.
Energy identities such as dissipation equals pressure drop times flow rate are free consistency checks.
Too large a penalty can worsen conditioning: the largest alpha is not automatically the best.
Central finite differences have truncation error of order h squared and round-off of order epsilon over h, so there is a best step.

understand.title: What each check protects
understand.text: The exact profile protects the state equation, the identity protects the objective, and the gradient check protects the link between them. If any one is wrong, an optimizer will still run and return a plausible-looking design, which is why the checks are done separately and first.

understand.title: The non-monotone mismatch
understand.text: Large alpha pushes the penalized region towards a true wall, which reduces leakage, but makes the discrete system stiffer near the boundary. On a fixed mesh the error outside therefore has a floor that moves with the mesh. The footnote's refinement test, which moves the minimum and lowers it, is the evidence that this is a numerical effect.

understand.title: Why the step size appears twice
understand.text: Two finite-difference steps agreeing with the analytic gradient to about 1e-10 rule out both a too-large step (truncation) and a too-small step (round-off) as the reason for the agreement.

steps.title: Brinkman channel equation
steps.note: 1D channel flow with a uniform penalty alpha and driving pressure gradient G.

steps.title: Exact solution
steps.note: As alpha goes to 0 this tends to the Poiseuille parabola G(H^2 - y^2)/(2 mu); as alpha grows the profile flattens into a plug with a thin wall layer of thickness 1/kappa.

steps.title: Energy identity
steps.note: Multiply the momentum equation by u and integrate by parts: the dissipation equals the power supplied by the pressure drop times the flow rate. The two bars in the figure are the two sides.

steps.title: Sensitivity of the dissipation
steps.note: For the dissipation objective with the state equation self-adjoint the total derivative reduces to the partial one, so the gradient is the integral of speed squared over the element. This is the quantity plotted in the left panel of the gradient check.

steps.title: Central difference and its best step
steps.note: Truncation shrinks with h and round-off grows as h shrinks, so there is a best step. Agreeing at two steps shows the analytic gradient is right.

steps.title: Relative error as the pass criterion
steps.note: The dotted reference line on the right-hand panel. The measured values of about 1e-10 sit four orders of magnitude below it.

worked.title: Check an exact Brinkman profile against the figure
worked.problem: Take the channel half-width H = 10 micrometres, viscosity mu = 1e-3 Pa s (assumed, water) and the pressure gradient that gives a Poiseuille peak of 0.005 m/s. Compute the centre velocity for alpha = 1e7 and compare with the orange curve.

solution.text: Pressure gradient from the Poiseuille peak.

worked.answer: About 0.0035 m/s, matching the orange curve. With the same viscosity, alpha = 3e6 gives about 0.0045 and alpha = 5e7 about 0.0016, matching the blue and red curves. The viscosity is inferred, not printed.

analyze.q: The mismatch minimum moves from alpha of about 1e4 to about 1e6 when the mesh is refined by a factor of two in size. What does that say about choosing a maximum alpha for an optimization?
analyze.hint: A mesh-dependent sweet spot, and continuation schemes.

analyze.q: Both finite-difference step sizes agree with the analytic gradient to about 1e-10, but the larger step is slightly worse. Why?
The identity errors are 0.08 and 0.18 percent for two viscous forms. Which would you expect to change if the mesh were refined, and why?

evaluate.q: Is passing the gradient check enough to trust an optimized design?
evaluate.hint: What else could be wrong: model, objective, local minima, mesh dependence.

evaluate.q: Is a 1 percent velocity mismatch against a body-fitted solution acceptable for a design study? How would you decide?
evaluate.hint: Relative to the effect size the design must resolve.

create: Redraw the right panel of the comparison with the footnote's finding as an annotation: arrows from the coarse to the fine minimum.
Design a continuation schedule for alpha that avoids the conditioning floor, and say what you would plot to show it works.

checks.q: Why does a large Brinkman penalty make a region act as a solid?
checks.answer: The term alpha u dominates, so the only way to balance the pressure gradient is for u to become very small.

checks.q: A gradient has relative error 1e-10 against finite differences. Does it pass the 1e-6 criterion?
checks.answer: Yes, by four orders of magnitude.

checks.q: Leak velocity falls monotonically with alpha but outside mismatch does not. How can both be true?
checks.hint: They measure different regions with different numerical effects.
checks.answer: Inside the penalized region the solution tends to zero, but on a fixed mesh the stiffer system near the boundary adds numerical error to the flow outside it.

checks.q: The two dissipation bars agree to 0.08 percent. Is the objective validated?
checks.hint: What is the agreement limited by?
checks.answer: It is consistent at the discretization-error level; refinement should reduce the difference further, which is the next evidence to ask for.

checks.q: How would you test the gradient of an objective with a different penalization law?
checks.answer: Pick several design variables, compute the analytic gradient, compare with central differences at two steps, and require relative error far below the criterion for both.
